s05m.slug: WEDNESDAY · 9:40 AM → 1:30 PM · BROUSSARD’S SEAFOOD, BANKS STREET — CHRISTMAS FOR A FISH MARKET
s05m.music: Mahalia Jackson — “Move On Up a Little Higher”
body: At twenty to ten on Ash Wednesday the line at Broussard’s goes out the door and along the front window and down Banks Street past the barbershop, and every forehead in it is marked. Some of the crosses are neat. Some are thumbprints. One, on a little boy holding a fistful of his grandmother’s coat, runs from his eyebrow up into his hair where he tried to rub it off and got caught. The sky over the street is low and white and hasn’t made up its mind about anything, and the bell over the door has quit ringing for each customer and settled into one long jangle.

Half of Mid-City is buying for Friday. Shrimp by the pound, heads on, in white paper. Catfish, whole and filleted. Crawfish for the weekend, the sacks by the walk-in door quieter than Monday’s. A man in a Knights of Columbus windbreaker wants forty pounds of drum for a fish fry at a church in Gentilly and wants it scaled, and Tony tells him scaled is Thursday, and the man says Thursday’s fine, and they shake on it over the case like two heads of state.

Tony works the register with the cordless phone jammed between his ear and his shoulder, writing Friday orders on the back of a paper sack with a carpenter’s pencil. There’s ice on the cuffs of his green market jacket and a smudge on his forehead, darker on the left where Hébert’s thumb pressed down. “Ten pounds, Mrs. Vo. Ten. No ma’am, I can’t hold you the big ones. It’s Lent. There’s no such thing as holding.”

Jack has the case. Gloria’s first rule is that nothing sits in its own water, and it holds on Banks Street the same as it holds over a Hobart in Marisol: he banks the shaved ice high at the back and low at the front, so the melt runs forward to the drain instead of pooling under the redfish, and lays the fish on it head to tail, and wraps, and weighs, and is back at the ice machine with the scoop every twenty minutes, because the case empties faster than he can fill it. The cotton gloves soak through by ten. By half past, his fingers have stopped reporting.

Under the front window Mr. Alcide opens oysters on his bench. The red radio on the shelf over him has WWOZ’s gospel hour on, and Mahalia Jackson is moving on up a little higher, slow, with the choir behind her, and Mr. Alcide goes right up with her in French, a half step behind and perfectly sure of himself.
At ten past eleven Miss Earline comes in under her plastic rain bonnet for a pound and the news. She gets the pound from Jack. She looks at his forehead while he wraps it.
“Father did yours,” she says.
“Yes ma’am.”

“I can tell. It leans to the Gospel side. Fifty years, every cross in this parish has had a little list to it.” She takes the shrimp and gives Tony the news across the register — the six o’clock was standing room, a Duplantis boy wore his Mardi Gras wig to it, the streetcar was full of dust — and then, with her change in her hand, looks back down the case at Jack. “And Lena’s going back out there with you.”
“Yes ma’am. All of us are.”
“Mm-hm,” says Miss Earline, and looks at Tony, and Tony looks at the register.
“You got your pound, Earline.”
“I got my pound,” she agrees, and ties her bonnet tighter under her chin, and goes out into the jangle with more news than she came in with.

Three and a half hours, and not one minute in them with room to think. He’s grateful. Ice, fish, paper, string, scale, the next one. Twice his right hand goes off on its own looking for the thing it has done after every hard hour since August, and finds the ice scoop instead, and he lets it have the scoop.

At a quarter past one Tony gives the register to the girl from the counter, a cousin of somebody’s, and comes down the length of the case wiping his hands on his apron, and tips his head at the walk-in. Jack follows him through the plastic strips. Tony pulls the steel door to behind them.

In here it’s February for real. One bulb in a wire cage, the compressor droning somewhere over their heads, boxes of Gulf shrimp packed in ice along the floor, and the drum laid out on its pallet, waiting for Thursday. The cold puts a little cloud in front of everything Tony says.

body.text: “Monday I asked you a question at the rail on Spanish Plaza in front of half of Mid-City.”
body.else: “Monday I asked you a question in this cooler.”

body: “I’m not asking it in my cooler.”
Jack’s hands are still wet from the case, and the cold goes straight into them. “I’d answer it if I could, Mr. Broussard.”
“I know you would.” Tony takes a crawfish sack off the stack, looks at it, and puts it back where it was. “That’s why I’m not asking.”
The compressor cuts out. In the quiet the sacks tick.

“I been watching phones all week,” Tony says. “Yours goes off, you take it out on the sidewalk. Hers goes off, she takes it out back by the shed and talks to the boil pot. Every time. I sell fish, son. I don’t do mysteries. But somebody on the other end of one of them phones is fixing to get some bad news.” He looks at the shrimp, at the drum, at the door. “Maybe two somebodies.”
There’s nothing Jack is allowed to say in here, and he doesn’t say it, and Tony nods at that like it was what he expected.

“Whoever it is,” Tony says. “You tell them to their face. Not on a phone. Not in a letter. Broussards do it to your face.” He points one thick finger at the floor of his own walk-in, the old knife scar white across the knuckle, as though the rule was poured in with the concrete.

He digs in his apron and comes out with a business card, and lays it flat against the steel wall, and writes on the back of it with the carpenter’s pencil from behind his ear, big square letters, bearing down hard enough to dent it.

body.title: A business card from Broussard’s, the back written on in carpenter’s pencil
body.text:
BROUSSARD’S SEAFOOD · BANKS STREET · NEW ORLEANS
—
FOR GLORIA. GULF SHRIMP, BROUSSARD PRICE. ASK FOR TONY.

body: He holds it out. “Who taught you ice? Gloria. You give her that.” He waits until it’s in Jack’s wet fingers. “Bring her.”

response: “Good.”
Tony puts his shoulder to the steel door and opens it on the warm and the line and Mahalia, and that’s the end of it. Jack dries the card on his shirt and puts it in his wallet behind his license.

At half past one Tony leaves the cousin the register and a list, hangs his apron on its nail, and drives Jack home to Dupre Street for the one meal with the heater on high and ice going to water on both their cuffs. He doesn’t say a word on the way. At the curb, with the engine running, he says, “I’ll be back for the van.”
Tony looks at him a long time in the cold, long enough for the little cloud in front of his mouth to come and go three times.
“Then you’re the only honest man in my cooler.”

Who, he leaves alone. He picks up a box of shrimp and carries it out ahead of Jack through the plastic strips, and at half past one he has his apron off and the cousin on the phone and Jack in the truck, and he drives to Dupre Street one-handed with his other arm out the window in February, like a man who has been told the one thing he needed. At the stop sign on Orleans he says, “Three o’clock,” and taps the wheel with his wedding ring.

choices.text: “Is that the rule? Whoever works your case on Ash Wednesday —”
response: “— is mine. Yeah.” Tony shoulders the door open. “I’m making it up. It’s still the rule.”

He’s pleased with himself the rest of the afternoon. He tells the cousin at the register, and Mr. Alcide over the oysters, and at half past one, with his apron on the nail, he tells the truck. He laughs about it again at the light on Broad, and when he pulls up on Dupre Street he leans across Jack and opens his door for him. “Don’t let her leave without me.”

s05h.slug: WEDNESDAY · 9:40 AM → 1:30 PM · DUPRE STREET — THE DAYBED
s05h.music: Mahalia Jackson — “Move On Up a Little Higher”
body: At twenty to ten Celeste is building a cooler on the oilcloth the way she would stock a crash cart: everything in reach, nothing where it doesn’t belong, and nothing touched that she hasn’t handed over. Jack has been handed the lid. He holds it.

Shrimp po’boys for tomorrow, the bread in one roll of butcher paper and the fried shrimp in another, because a po’boy dressed on Wednesday is a soggy disgrace by Thursday and she has standards even for Texas. A paper sack of Plaquemines satsumas, the leaves still on two of them. Pralines in wax paper. A thermos of coffee with THURSDAY on a strip of tape around its middle.
“Today you fast,” Celeste says. “That’s for tomorrow. If anybody opens that thermos in Louisiana, I’ll know.”

body.text: Last of all, a Tupperware with KEVIN on the lid in her own marker: what’s left of the lemon pound cake, wedged in at an angle so it rides flat.
Last of all, a Tupperware with KEVIN on the lid in Laney’s silver Sharpie, a crown drawn over the V: what’s left of the lemon pound cake, wedged in at an angle so it rides flat.

Then she takes the pie tin with the boysenberry ghost still in the corner down off the top of the refrigerator, washed and dried since the night they came, and opens Mémère’s cedar box on the sideboard, and fills the tin with pralines. One at a time. Each one in its own square of wax paper, laid in flat, edge to edge, the next row on top of the first.
body.else: Then she takes Gloria’s pecan tin down off the top of the refrigerator, washed and dried since the night they came, and opens Mémère’s cedar box on the sideboard, and fills the tin with pralines. One at a time. Each one in its own square of wax paper, laid in flat, edge to edge, the next row on top of the first.

body: Jack holds the lid and watches his debt to Gloria get paid off in sugar by a woman he met a week and a half ago.
“A tin goes back full, baby.” Celeste presses its lid on with the heel of her hand. “That’s not manners. That’s law.”

She tears a sheet of butcher paper off the roll, for the satsumas, and folds it, and with her eyes on the fold and her voice just above a whisper, she says, “I’ve been a nurse thirty years.” Another fold. “I know what a person looks like the morning after they’ve decided something.” She runs her thumbnail down the crease. “I don’t need to know what.” She takes the cooler lid out of his hands and puts it on and snaps both latches. “Do it right.”

She doesn’t wait to see what he’ll say, and he doesn’t say anything, and at ten o’clock she has the okra on the board and the onions going in the black pot for half past one, and the kitchen is a kitchen again.

Through the doorway to the front room he can see the end of the foldout where the girls have slept all week, and Lena’s bag open on it. She packs by sections, the way she argues. The black dress from this morning, folded in thirds. The jean jacket hung on the doorknob with its chest pocket buttoned down. She doesn’t come into the kitchen while he’s in it. He doesn’t go into the front room. Twice she passes the doorway with her arms full, and the second time he’s looking, and her back goes a little straighter going by.

The third time she stops on the far side of it to shake out the mantilla before she folds it, and holds it up to the window by two corners, and the gray light comes through the lace onto her face. She hasn’t washed. The cross Hébert gave her is still on her forehead, a little crooked, the same as his. He stands in the kitchen with a roll of butcher paper in his hands and looks at it across two rooms, at that and at the dark place in the lace where her hair has been, and does not go to the doorway, and it costs what he knew it would, and he pays it.
At eleven Remy comes down the attic ladder in his sunglasses and lies on the linoleum in front of the stove because it’s warm there, and asks if a man can die of Lent.
“Not on the first day,” Celeste says, stepping over him with the okra. “Get up. You’re in my light.”

At noon EWTN rings the Angelus in the front room, and Mémère, on the daybed in her black with her ashes on and a blanket over her knees, says it along with the television in French, half a word ahead of the priest in Alabama. When it’s done she says something to Lena, and Lena lifts the lid of the old console and sets a record on it and puts the needle down, and Mahalia Jackson comes out of the speakers into the house, slow and enormous, like weather. Mémère closes her eyes to listen to it. She opens them on Jack, in the kitchen doorway, and crooks one finger.
He crosses. It’s four steps to the daybed. Lena takes a sweater off the pile on the foldout and goes and stands in the far doorway, the one to the hall, with it folded over her arm.

Mémère has a holy card for him, its corners gone soft as cloth: Saint Joseph, with the lilies and the Child and a carpenter’s square at his feet. She turns it over to show him the back. The nineteenth of March is his birthday. She has had it from Celeste, who had it from Lena.

body.title: A holy card, the corners soft
body.text:
SAINT JOSEPH · PRIEZ POUR NOUS
(on the back, in an old woman’s pencil) le 19 mars

body: She keeps hold of it after he’s taken it, so they’re both holding it, and talks. A good deal of it. Her French goes low and quick and level, the way she says the rosary, with Joseph’s name in it twice and a short dry laugh in the middle at somebody’s expense, and at the end she lets go of the card and taps his wrist with one finger and says one last thing, and is done.
Jack looks at the far doorway.
Lena shakes the sweater out and folds it again. “She says Joseph was a good man.”
He has been in this house eleven days. He knows about how long French runs in English. It doesn’t come out that short.

response: Mémère corrects his *r* — twice, the second time with her eyes shut, as if it pains her — and then pats his cheek two times with a hand like paper left out in the sun. In the hall doorway Lena holds the sweater against her stomach with both arms.

At half past one they eat the one meal at the oilcloth, Celeste’s shrimp and okra over rice and not a scrap of meat in the house, and Remy is given grace as a penance and gets lost in it between *bless us* and *bounty*. Tony comes in from the market in his apron, eats standing up at the counter, kisses his wife, and is back in the truck by two.
Lena folds the sweater again, though it’s already folded. “Drive safe.” She doesn’t look up from it.
Mémère looks from one of them to the other, and closes her eyes, and listens to Mahalia.

Tony comes in from Banks Street at twenty-five past one with ice on his cuffs and his apron still on under his jacket, and they eat at half past: Celeste’s shrimp and okra, no meat, the table quiet with hunger. Remy says grace and rushes it, and Celeste makes him say it again slower. By two the truck is gone back to the market and the pot is soaking in the sink.
Mémère, who understood that perfectly well in English, says, “*Menteur.*”
In the hall doorway Lena laughs without any sound at all, the sweater up over her mouth, and stops.

At half past one Remy says grace over Celeste’s shrimp and okra and finishes it, out of habit, with the prayer for the faithful departed. “Nobody’s dead, Remy,” Celeste says. “I am,” says Remy. Tony, in from the market, eats fast and says it’s the best she’s made, which he says every Ash Wednesday, and is gone again by two.

s06.slug: WEDNESDAY · 2:40 PM · N. DUPRE STREET, THE CURB — SEND-OFF

body.text: Tony has had him home since half past one, ice still on both their cuffs, for the one meal, and gone back to Banks Street for the afternoon.
body.else: The shrimp and okra he watched Celeste start at ten has been eaten, at half past one, the one meal, and the pot is soaking.

body: At half past two the twins come up the walk from school with their uniforms untucked and their ashes still on. Josie’s is half gone, rubbed off on her sleeve, which is gray to the elbow. Jude’s is perfect. He has carried it home all day like a full cup.

Kevin’s mother’s Odyssey stands at the curb with its hatch up and WHO DAT on the back glass in white shoe polish, and Laney, on her knees on the bumper with the bottle, adds a dot after it and then, in careful block letters, 40 DAYS, and gets down and looks at it with her head on one side.
On the dash, under a strip of Celeste’s tape, Kevin has put up the sheet for the way home.

body.title: Taped to the dash of the Odyssey, in Kevin’s capitals
body.text:
RETURN — DUPRE ST. → MARISOL
KEVIN: Dupre → Houston
MARGOT: Houston → San Antonio
JACK: San Antonio → Ft. Stockton (THEO NAV.)
FT. STOCKTON: SLEEP 2 HRS. EVERYBODY.
KEVIN: Ft. Stockton → Tucson
THEO: Tucson → Blythe
KEVIN: Blythe → home
RESPECTFULLY — K.

body: Laney opens the glovebox and puts Coco in it, fleur-de-lis up, and closes it with both hands.
“I am not riding two thousand miles with a coconut in front of my knees,” Theo says from the middle row.
“She’s not *a* coconut, Theodore.”

Margot goes up the porch steps to say goodbye to Mémère the way she would say goodbye to a department chair, hand out, and Mémère ignores the hand and pulls her down by it and kisses her on both cheeks. Margot submits with her arms at her sides and her glasses knocked crooked, and comes back down the steps a little pink, and gets into the passenger seat, and opens the atlas to Louisiana, and says, “That was not in the literature.”

Theo is sitting sideways in his chair with the door open and his sunglasses on, looking at the house. He has been up since before Jack was. He looks at the porch and the swing and the shed out back with its brown line around the boards at four and a half feet, the year the water came, and says, without taking the sunglasses off, “Eleven days. It was a Fellini picture. Three courses at every meal and somebody always singing.” There’s no topper. He keeps looking at the house.
Lena comes down the walk with her duffel and stops at the hatch, where Kevin is fitting the bags in by a system only he understands.
“Way-back,” she says.
Kevin clicks a pen and writes it at the bottom of the sheet without a word. Jack’s chair is the right one in the middle, where the sheet puts him.

Remy has come out on the porch in his sunglasses with a mug of black coffee, the one thing he’s allowed, and comes down off the steps to hug Jack one-armed, two slaps on the back, the second harder. “Forty days,” he says. “That’s what I gave. After that, Ohio, if you’re still —” He looks past Jack at the van, at the hatch, at his sister, and takes his sunglasses off and puts them back on. “Forty days.”

Luc is up, which is a surprise. He worked the Bourbon detail till two in the morning and he’s standing on the walk in a T-shirt and sweatpants with a coffee, and he shakes Jack’s hand once, the cop’s handshake, short and dry. “Drive the limit in Texas.” His eyes go to the open stretch of sidewalk between Jack and his sister at the side door, and rest there, and come back, and he drinks his coffee.
Jude stands in front of Jack with his perfect cross and his book bag still on both shoulders.

body.text: “Is it soon yet?”
“Is it yet?”
“Is Canada still far?”
“Did you ever tell yours?”

body: “Tuesday,” Jack says.
Jude thinks about it and nods, man to man, and hitches his book bag up and goes inside, satisfied.
Josie has the porch rail. She sits on it with her knees up and her gray sleeve and her eyes on the curb.

body.text: “We’re not at the table now.”
“You’re not in college *now*. You’re on the curb.”
“You looked at your plate. I saw.”

body: And then, so the whole curb can hear it: “So. Lena or the girl in Canada.”

Laney stops with the shoe polish. Kevin stops with a bag. At the van’s side door Lena goes on fitting her small bag in under the way-back seat, and it takes her exactly as long as it would have taken anyway.

choices.text: “Ask me at Easter. You’ll be the first one I answer.”
choices.key: On the curb on Dupre Street Josie asked again who you’re going to marry. You told her to ask you at Easter, and she’d be the first one you answered.
response: Josie looks at him from the rail, solemn as a notary. “Easter,” she says. “I’m writing it down.”

She does. She takes a pen out of her uniform pocket and writes it on the back of her hand, EASTER, in letters that get smaller toward the knuckles, and blows on it, and holds it up at him so he can see it’s official.

choices.text: “Then I still can’t answer it, Josie. I’m sorry.”
choices.key: On the curb on Dupre Street Josie asked again who you’re going to marry. You told her you still couldn’t answer it, and that you were sorry.
response: “That’s *three* times,” Josie says.

She isn’t angry. She holds up three fingers at him from the rail and folds them down one at a time, keeping the book, and when she gets to the fist she looks at it for a while as though the answer might be in there after all.

choices.key: On the curb on Dupre Street Josie asked again who you’re going to marry. You told her to go ask somebody who knows everything.

response.text: “I *told* her,” Josie says. “She says it counts.”
response.else: “She says it only counts if you carry something,” Josie says.

response: Then she looks at the van, and at the way-back, where her sister is still bent over the seat, and doesn’t say the next thing. On Josie that is a miracle.

choices.text: “Ask Mémère. She’s been right all week.”
choices.key: On the curb on Dupre Street Josie asked again who you’re going to marry. You told her to go ask somebody who knows everything.
response: Josie turns around on the rail and calls something into the house in French, and listens, and turns back.
“Mémère says *ask him at Easter*.”
Jack hasn’t heard anybody answer. He looks at Josie. Josie looks back at him with her gray sleeve and her half a cross and gives away nothing at all.

s06a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:05 PM · N. DUPRE STREET — THE PORCH, AND THE MIRROR
body: Mémère has been brought out to the porch in her black, with her ashes and her blanket and her chair, to see them off properly, and when Jack comes up the steps she takes his sleeve and says something to him in French, short this time, with her chin up.
Josie, on the rail, translates every word. “She says the dust looks good on you.” She listens to the rest. “She says it’s the first honest thing you’ve worn all week.”
Mémère lets go of his sleeve and folds her hands on the blanket, and that’s the last word on it, in either language.

body.text: Celeste has the cooler open on the curb. She lifts the po’boys aside to show him the pie tin with the boysenberry ghost still in the corner, washed, and full to the lid with Mémère’s pralines in their squares of wax paper. “For your Gloria,” she says. “A tin goes back full, baby. That’s not manners, that’s law.”

Celeste has the cooler open on the curb. She lifts the po’boys aside to show him Gloria’s pecan tin, washed, and full to the lid with Mémère’s pralines in their squares of wax paper. “For your Gloria,” she says. “A tin goes back full, baby. That’s not manners, that’s law.”
Celeste checks the latches on the cooler one more time, with the tin riding full under the po’boys where she put it, and pats the lid twice, a nurse finishing a dressing.

body: Then, low, to him and nobody else: “You call your mother when you get there. A mother wants to hear it from you.”
“Yes ma’am.”
She looks at the two of them, him at the porch steps and her daughter at the far end of the van with her hand on the side door, and says, “Hm.”

Laney gets to her next, with her pink train case under one arm and her sunglasses pushed up into her hair, and holds on to her with her eyes shut. “Mrs. Broussard, I am naming my first daughter after you,” Laney says into her shoulder, “and my second one after your gumbo.” Celeste pats her back the way she would burp a baby, briskly, twice, and says, “Get in the van, baby, you’ll miss Texas.”

body.text: Kevin is last, because he’s been loading. Celeste takes his face in both hands and looks at it. “You slept under this roof on your birthday,” she says. “You know what that makes you.” Kevin says, “Yes ma’am,” and nothing else, and she lets go of his face, and he goes around to the driver’s side and gets in and checks the mirrors, all three, twice.

body: Tony’s truck comes round the corner from Orleans at three on the dot and stops in the middle of Dupre Street with the engine running, and Tony gets down in his market jacket and leaves the door open.

body.text: “Ohio.” He puts his hand out, and Jack takes it, and the handshake turns into the hug halfway through without asking anybody, Tony’s cold cuffs on the back of his neck. “Bring her,” Tony says into his ear, and lets him go.
body.else: He hugs Jack without a handshake first, hard, fish and ice and Old Spice. “Monday I asked you a question,” he says, with his hands on Jack’s shoulders. “Today I’m not asking. You come back, whichever one you are.”

body: Lena goes back up the walk. Jack stands at the van’s open door, out of the way, and watches the Broussards say goodbye to her.

Celeste holds her by the back of the head and says something into her hair that nobody else is meant to hear, and nobody does. Mémère reaches up from the chair and puts her fingertips on the medal on its mended chain, and keeps them there a while, her lips moving. Tony picks her up off the porch step under the arms like she’s nine years old and a king just waved at her off a float, and sets her down a step lower, and wipes his face with the back of his wrist. The twins come down the walk on either side of her, at her elbows, Josie talking and Jude not.

She has washed her face. Jack can see the water still at her hairline. She washed all of it but her forehead, and the cross Hébert put there is still there, crooked to the Gospel side. She gets into the van by the far door and climbs over into the way-back without a look at the middle row.

Kevin turns the key. The whole house is on the porch: Celeste with her arms folded, Tony with his hand up, Mémère in her chair, Remy on the steps, Luc in the doorway with his coffee, Jude beside him, Josie up on the rail. And Clovis, leaning on the porch post with a Kool behind his ear he isn’t lighting till they’re gone, starts the first verse of “Just a Closer Walk with Thee,” off-key and slow, as Kevin pulls away from the curb, and the rest of the porch doesn’t join in, because Clovis knows the first verse of everything and the rest of nothing, and the porch has learned to let him.

In the side mirror the clothesline in the side yard goes by, and on it, pinned by their rolled tops, the gold bags from Fat Tuesday in a row, LARGE among them, turning a little on the line in the wind with their eyeholes, watching the van go.

s07.slug: WEDNESDAY · 4:30 PM · I-10 WEST, THE MISSISSIPPI AT BATON ROUGE — FORTY DAYS
body: The bridge at Baton Rouge goes up over the river in a long gray hump, and the Mississippi goes by under it brown and wide and indifferent, the other way from last time, and then they’re down on the far side among the cane fields, cut to stubble now, the color gone out of everything but the sky.

Kevin drives with both hands. Margot has the passenger seat and the atlas open on her knees to Louisiana, though they won’t need it till El Paso. Theo and Jack have the two middle chairs. Laney and Lena have the way-back. The radio is off and stays off. It’s a van full of people after Mass, the quiet on the church steps before anybody lights up or says what they thought of the homily, and Jack, who has nothing to light, sits in it with his hands between his knees, rubbing his thumb back and forth along the seam of his jeans until the denim is warm.
In the rearview mirror, six foreheads, every one of them smudged.
“Okay,” Laney says from the back. “Okay, okay, okay. It’s up.” She leans forward between the middle chairs and holds her pink BlackBerry up over the seats so the van can see it.

body.name: Laney Price
body.text: six sinners and a coconut. remember you are dust (but moisturize)
body.meta: Wednesday at 4:31pm via BlackBerry · 3 people like this

body: “Tagging y’all,” Laney says.
“Don’t tag me,” Lena says.
“Why.”
“I won’t see it.”
There’s a small silence in the way-back. “…*Why* won’t you see it.”
“I gave it up.”
Laney lowers the phone.

“I’m sorry,” she says. “I’m sorry, I just — no. No ma’am. You don’t give up *Facebook*. People give up chocolate. People give up *Diet Coke*. Facebook is the *news*, Magdalena. What you’re describing is a *disappearance*. It’s witness protection. Forty days! Do you know what happens in forty days? People get engaged in forty days. People get *divorced*. Somebody’s going to have a baby and you won’t know if it’s a boy. Somebody’s going to change their —” She stops. “— their *picture*, and you’re going to walk around Marisol like Rip Van Winkle in a mantilla. How are you going to *know* anything? How is anybody going to know you *know*? This is the most selfish thing I have ever heard of a Catholic doing, and I took AP European History.”

Margot has the visor down against the sun, which is low and straight ahead now and will be till dark, and in the little mirror on the back of it Jack can see Theo’s face, and behind it, from the way-back, Laney’s. Their eyes meet in the glass. It lasts no time at all, and he knows exactly what it is. He has known since the levee last night, when it got a name. He keeps his face where it is. In the rearview, past Kevin’s ear, he catches Lena keeping hers.
Lena folds her hands on her knees.

“It’s Facebook,” she says, to the van, the way she’d read a docket. “It’s every Friday on bread and water, the old way. It’s the Stations at St. Brendan’s, every Friday night. That’s my Lent. It isn’t up for discussion, and it isn’t up for comment.”
“Bread and water’s not the minimum, Lena,” Kevin says, to the windshield.
“I’m not a minimum kind of girl, Kevin.”

“Durkheim has a name for this.” Margot doesn’t look up from Louisiana. “The negative cult. The rites of abstention. What you won’t eat, what you won’t say, what you won’t do on which days. You’ve all agreed to be holier by subtraction.” She turns a page to Texas. “It’s very efficient.”
“Durkheim never went a day without lunch in his life,” Lena says.
“Durkheim was a rabbi’s son. I imagine he fasted plenty.” Margot turns another page. “Then he stopped, and wrote it up.”
“Then he knew what it costs, and he still called it a rite.” In the rearview Jack can see a slice of her: one eye, the ash, the window behind her going by. “Good. It is one. Write that up.”
“And you got ashes,” Theo says.
“Participant observation.”
“Sweets,” Kevin says, unprompted, in the voice he uses for medical histories. “No sweets until Easter. Bà Nội’s rule, since I was seven. Family history of it.”
“Carbs,” Laney says, sitting back. “In solidarity. I’m a lapsed Baptist, I don’t have to give up a thing, so it counts *double*.” A pause. “Until Phoenix.”
“Phoenix is tomorrow,” says Margot.
“Then it’s going to be a very *intense* Lent.”
Theo has his forehead against the window, watching a crop duster’s hangar go by in a field of nothing. “Kevin says I already gave something up.”
Kevin drives. His eyes stay on the road, and the road stays straight.
“What about you, Father Jack?” Theo says, his forehead still on the glass.
“Cigarettes.”
“We *know*, sugar,” says Laney. “Louisiana knows.”
And there are Fridays.

Lent on Glenwood Avenue was Mrs. Paul’s fish sticks and a can of peas, and the fish fry in the basement at St. Brigid’s with Frank at a folding table eating three plates of perch because it was the only time all year a Costigan got to be pious and full at once. On Glenwood Avenue bread and water was for the Little Flower and the Desert Fathers. Nonna did it, in Calabria, as a girl, and told it like a war story. He hasn’t eaten since the shrimp and okra and his stomach knows it, and his hands want the thing they want, and somewhere behind him a girl just read her Lent into the record like she was daring God to find a hole in it, and he hasn’t said his Fridays to anybody yet.

choices.key: On the drive home you said out loud you’d fast every Friday of Lent on bread and water, the way Lena does. Nobody asked you, she said.
response: From the way-back, her eyes on her own hands: “Nobody asked you, Youngstown.”

“Oh, *Lord*,” Laney says. “It’s a *competition*.” She flops back against the seat with her phone face down on her stomach, her Lent personally ruined by both of them, and in the rearview Lena is looking out the back glass at Louisiana going away behind WHO DAT, with the corner of her mouth exactly where it was.

choices.key: On the drive home you decided, without telling anybody, to fast every Friday of Lent on bread and water.
response: He doesn’t say it. He decides it, there in the middle chair with the cane fields going by, bread and water every Friday till Easter, and it’s devotion and it’s pride, both at once, the wanting to give God something and the wanting to keep up with her, and he can’t pull one out of the other and doesn’t try. He’ll take that one to a priest. Behind him, in the way-back, Laney is explaining to Lena how a person could check Facebook *only for emergencies*, and Lena is saying no.

choices.text: “Bread and water. That’s a Tuesday in Ohio.”
choices.key: On the drive home you told the van you’d do bread and water on Fridays too, and called it a Tuesday in Ohio.
response: Theo laughs into the window. Laney says, “He’s *joking*. Look at him. He’s not joking.”
“That’s not true,” Kevin says, eyes on the road, “and you know it’s not true.”

From the way-back, nothing. Not even *Youngstown*. He looks in the rearview, and she’s looking out the back glass at the river going away behind WHO DAT, and the nothing goes on past the next exit, and he feels all of it.
